analysis.one_liner: Limits how much people hurt by defective products can recover from manufacturers and sellers.
analysis.headline: The House never voted on the bill; it sat in the Judiciary Committee, the record points to a companion bill for further action, and it died when the Congress ended in January 1997.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have set national rules for lawsuits over defective products, overriding state law on the issues it covers. It would shield stores and other non-manufacturer sellers from most liability, bar most claims about products sold more than 15 years earlier, make each defendant pay only its own share of pain-and-suffering damages, and cap punitive damages at the greater of $250,000 or three times the financial losses, with a higher burden of proof. It would also give defendants a complete defense if an injured person was drunk or on drugs and more than half responsible for the accident.
analysis.who_benefits: Manufacturers of consumer and industrial products, plus retailers, distributors, and other sellers, who would face far less exposure to product-injury lawsuits. Liability insurers would pay out less. Under the seller rules, a store that sells a dangerous product could only be sued if it was careless, broke its own warranty, or acted intentionally — not simply because the product it sold was defective.

how_it_helps.text: A product seller who is not the manufacturer would be liable only if the injured person proves the seller was careless, broke its own express warranty, or engaged in intentional wrongdoing — removing ordinary seller liability for defective products [S2].
Being drunk or under the influence of drugs, and more than 50 percent responsible for the accident, would be a complete defense that wipes out the injured person's claim entirely [S2].
Each defendant would pay only its own proportionate share of noneconomic losses like pain and suffering, instead of being jointly responsible for the full amount [S2].
Most product liability claims would be barred unless filed within 15 years of the product's delivery, with an exception for chronic illness [S2].

Punitive damages would require clear and convincing evidence of intent to harm or conscious, flagrant indifference to safety, and would be capped at the greater of $250,000 or three times the economic loss — applied by the judge without being disclosed to the jury [S2].
The bill would supersede state law on every issue it covers, replacing the varying state rules that govern these cases today [S2].

analysis.who_pays: People injured or killed by defective products, whose compensation would be lower or unavailable: capped punitive damages, several-only liability for pain and suffering, a 15-year filing deadline, a near-total shield for sellers, and a total bar for intoxicated claimants. When one defendant cannot pay its share, the shortfall falls on the injured person.

drawbacks.text: Several-only liability for pain and suffering means that if a share of the fault belongs to a company that is bankrupt or beyond the court's reach, the injured person simply loses that share of compensation [S2].

The punitive damages cap — the greater of $250,000 or three times economic loss — would be applied by the court and hidden from the jury, and the clear-and-convincing standard is a much higher bar than ordinary civil proof, so the hardest-to-punish corporate misconduct would draw smaller penalties [S2].

The 15-year limit runs from delivery of the product, so long-latent defects could be time-barred even though the bill carves out chronic illness; the preemption clause overrides state laws that currently give consumers stronger remedies [S2].
A complete defense for claimants more than 50 percent responsible due to intoxication would bar recovery even where a genuinely defective product caused the harm.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's stated rationale is that inconsistent state liability rules raise costs for businesses and prices for consumers, and that sellers should not answer for defects in products they did not make. Those arguments have force for the seller-liability provision, which retains an exception when the manufacturer cannot be found or sued. But the core effect of the bill is to reduce what injured people can recover — through the damages cap, the higher proof standard, several liability, and the filing deadline — and shift those costs onto the people hurt and their families. The bill is well drafted for its purpose, but its purpose runs against claimants.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced in February 1995 and sent to the House Judiciary Committee, it was never brought up; a month later the record pointed to companion bill H.R. 956 for further action, and the bill died when the Congress ended in January 1997.

narrative.text: Rep. Henry Hyde introduced the bill on February 15, 1995, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on the Judiciary [S1].

On March 15, 1995, the action record states 'For Further Action See H.R.956' — the House treated a companion product liability bill as the vehicle for the idea, and H.R. 955 itself never advanced [S5].
No committee vote, floor vote, or further action ever occurred on H.R. 955 before the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997 [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never advanced, people injured by defective products kept whatever right to sue and recover their state law provides, and manufacturers, sellers, and insurers did not get the federal liability limits this bill would have created. The bill's substance lived on separately in H.R. 956, per the House record itself.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Injured consumers kept state-law lawsuit rights

for.name: Rep. Henry Hyde
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on February 15, 1995; it was referred to the Judiciary Committee, which he chaired

against.name: House Committee on the Judiciary
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Never reported the bill out or scheduled action; the record instead pointed to companion bill H.R. 956

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken on the bill and it had no cosponsors, so no party split appears anywhere in the record.

industries.industry: Manufacturers of consumer and industrial products
industries.note: The bill would cap their punitive damages exposure, require a higher burden of proof, and impose a 15-year filing limit, cutting payments to people hurt by their products. The savings come out of injured people's compensation.

industries.industry: Retailers, distributors, and other product sellers
industries.note: Sellers would be liable only for their own carelessness, their own warranty, or intentional wrongdoing — not for selling a defective product. A narrow exception keeps sellers on the hook when the manufacturer cannot be sued or a judgment against it cannot be collected.
Lower and more predictable liability for product injuries means smaller payouts on product liability policies. The cost falls on the injured people whose claims would shrink or disappear.

The bill would shrink and cap the claims that injured people can bring, shrinking the contingency-fee bar along with them. Its business would only have existed because injured people had claims worth bringing.
